reading.body:
The Business Roundtable's 17 AI lobbying filings name 26 lobbyists, and 10 of them appear on all 17, so this is a standing team rather than a per-issue hire.

The distribution is steep. Ten lobbyists carry the full 17 filings, two more carry 14, and the remaining 14 people appear on between one and 11. A large share of the names are occasional, brought in for particular filings. The two bills named, HR 633 and S 146, are the only legislative targets the data identifies, and both appear in filings from 2025 or later.

For AI specifically, this is the trade-association layer of policy work. The Business Roundtable is a membership body for large employers, so its AI lobbying represents the collective position of its members rather than one compute or power developer. The filings show who is doing that work and how consistently, which is the part of lobbying that is public. They do not show what was argued, what was spent, or whether any bill moved.

What the data does not cover is the substance. A filing reports that a client lobbied on an issue, not the position taken, and nothing here ties these filings to data centers, electricity procurement, or grid policy. The connection between AI lobbying and the physical buildout is not visible in this record.
